A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CFT research, with matching core experiments and identifiable correspondence between sections and appendices. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V2 reports original BERT sentiment-classification experiments on modified Amazon and Yelp data, including five-seed F1 results, ablations, and sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds stronger-noise comparisons, an identical-view ablation, layer sensitivity results, and statistical tests.

M1.justification: Section 5 revises the reported Φ construction from the patch average itself to a jointly learned MLP applied to that average. The supervised-loss expression also changes from p(r1|x) to p(y|x). The core two-view alignment and batch-shuffled adjustment algorithms are retained; these revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Amazon/Yelp sentiment classification and both injection mechanisms remain unchanged. V3 extends input-condition coverage to 4× and 8× spurious-noise intensity in Table 1, beyond the original intensity and doubled/tripled cases already examined in v2.

E2.justification: V3 adds SWA and WISE to both Yelp and Amazon comparisons in Experiment 1. V2 evaluated them only in Experiment 2. This substantially strengthens the first experiment's comparator set, particularly because SWA exceeds CFT on its original OOD settings. The WSA-to-SWA spelling correction is not a new method.

E3.justification: The original backbone, F1 metric, sampling, validation split, and training budget are retained. Added experimental designs use 4×/8× noise, replace paired views with identical (R1, R1) views, and extract Φ from the embedding, first, fifth, tenth, and last layers.

E4.justification: V3 adds substantive tests of three questions: whether CFT surpasses SWA under stronger injected noise, whether distinct views are necessary, and how Φ extraction depth affects robustness. These appear in Tables 1, 2, and 6. The earlier spuriousness, training-size, and inference-sampling analyses remain in Appendix H.

E5.justification: Beyond the retained five-seed means and boxplots, Appendix G introduces pairwise paired t-tests for Experiment 2 at 90%, 70%, and 50% correlation, with three p-value tables. Table 6 separately specifies three seeds for the new layer study; no increase in the original experiments' run counts is reported.

E6.justification: All original main-table result rows and Figures 4–9 are retained. New results materially qualify the comparison: at 10% correlation on the original Amazon task, SWA scores 59.75 versus CFT's 56.40, while CFT leads under the added 4×/8× conditions. V3 also adds identical-view, layer-sensitivity, and statistical-test outcomes.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.5 changes deterministic identification of C into learning a stable-component representation satisfying approximate cross-view agreement. The dependency explanation below Assumption 4.2 is corrected from S0/S1 to R0/R1. The central adjustment formula and Theorem 4.6's appendix proof are retained; its added expectation expression is equivalent.

C1.justification: V2 presents causal fine-tuning as identifying causal components under the proposed assumptions. V3 substantially narrows the practical claim: the SCM supplies an identification-guided inductive bias, and learned representations are proxies rather than recovered ground-truth causal variables. The abstract and contribution statements adopt this revised framing.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive qualifications about the SCM's abstract status, imperfect assumptions in injected data, feature-selection judgments, and failure with indistinguishable or misaligned views. It also explains SWA's competitiveness and the stronger-noise findings. Appendix G introduces an overly broad significance interpretation that is not supported against every comparator.

D1.justification: V3 adds an explicit code/data release statement and repository link, specifies K = 20 for reported adjustment results, and explains shuffling as empirical-marginal Monte Carlo sampling without label conditioning. Most architecture details and both appendix algorithms were already documented in v2; the PDFs do not establish an underlying sampling-setting change.

R1.justification: V3 adds recent work by Shaib et al., Han et al., Zhou and Zhu, and Li et al., plus deep-learning references supporting feature-depth motivation. Yu's 2023 thesis and Yuan et al.'s 2023 benchmark paper disappear. The existing transportability and causal-representation-learning positioning is largely retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodological explanations, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. The controlled-benchmark discussion moves from Section 6.3 to Appendix C, and new explanatory appendices reorganize the narrative. The title, authorship information, publication header, acknowledgments, and impact statement also change.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws the motivating example and CFT pipeline, and combines the original and refined causal graphs in Figure 2. Tables 1 and 2 gain subtables, and Tables 3–6 are added. Existing result plots are retained but resized or relocated.

improvement.justification: V3 improves transparency through previously missing strong comparisons, direct tests of view and layer assumptions, and clearer separation between idealized identification and practical proxy learning. These help readers assess CFT's scope and weaknesses. The gains are limited by remaining overstatements: Appendix G's broad significance claim at 70% correlation is unsupported against SFT (p = 0.092) and SWA (p = 0.969).
